persons.name: Robert Allen Kinzie

occupation.note: 'The Kinzies, John and Robert A., merchants' in the 1833 roster. Andreas: he 'remained in Chicago when the rest of the family left in the spring of 1831, and early in 1832 erected a frame store on the West Side - the first frame store in Chicago - and probably the first frame building, aside from the one erected by Government for Billy Caldwell in 1828.'

persons.note: HE IS THE REASON CHARLES BUTLER AND ARTHUR BRONSON CAME WEST, which is the best-documented chain of causation in the whole 1833-35 record. Butler's letter of 1881: Bronson called on the New York Indian-goods merchant Daniel Jackson for information about Chicago, and Jackson 'said that he would then introduce him to a man from Chicago, who at that moment happened to be in his store making purchases of Indian goods. This was Robert A. Kinzie.' Kinzie offered them his quarter interest in the north fractional half of Section 10 - the ground Kinzie's Addition was laid out on. He was also a candidate at the first town election of 10 August 1833 and took nine votes, the highest of any unsuccessful candidate. THE TOWN'S OWN ROLLS, 1833-1835 — CORROBORATION, NOT A GRADE. The early Chicago voter and tax lists held by the Illinois Regional Archives Depository name this person 2 times: Poll list of the first election of the Board of Trustees of the Town of Chicago, 10 August 1833 — “Kinzie, R. A.” (poll_1833_018, line 39); Tax list of the Town of Chicago, 1833 — “Kinzie, Robert A.” (tax_1833_063, line 115). These are the town's own contemporary paper rather than a recollection of it, and each appearance says that a man of that name stood on that roll in that year — no more. The reading is twice mediated (Schulz's transcription, then Genealogy Trails' republication) and this project has not seen the IRAD originals. Under the ratified ladder (T-0513) the 1835 poll with a second independent source is attested, the 1835 poll alone or a 1833/1834 list with another source is inferred, and a single appearance with nothing else is a projected resident. This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE — T-0515 applies the ladder against every source at once. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: one resident of the surname 'Kinzie' agrees with the entry's forenames; 4 bearer(s) of the surname were considered. (data/research/civic/voter_crosswalk.json). FERGUS 1839'S LATER LISTS — 1837 AND 1839 EVIDENCE, NEVER AN 1835 FACT. Fergus' Chicago Directory for 1839 names this person 1 time in its two later lists: the poll of Chicago's first city election, 2 May 1837 — “Robert A. Kinzie” (f1839_v0652, printed page 46, ward 6, voting for John H. Kinzie). What a match may carry, and it is short: that the man was in Chicago on 2 May 1837 and in that ward. It is written as 1837 evidence with describes_date 1837-05-02, never as an 1835 fact, and the person's grade does not move on this alone. Under the ratified ladder a second contemporary source is what lifts projected_resident, and a poll twenty-two months after the scene date is a second source about CONTINUED RESIDENCE, not about July 1835. The ward is a location in the CITY of 1837, whose six wards are drawn on printed page 46; it is not a location in the town of 1835 and does not place a house. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: Surname 'Kinzie' folds to the same string as the 1837 entry's, and the given name of both begins R. (data/research/directories/fergus_1839_election_crosswalk_1835.json and fergus_1839_register_crosswalk_1835.json). This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE. Under the ratified ladder (T-0513) a second independent source is what lifts a projected resident, and a poll twenty-two months after the scene date — or a register four years after it — is a second source about CONTINUED RESIDENCE rather than about July 1835. T-0515 applies the ladder against every source at once; this pass hands it the evidence and not the verdict. THE FEDERAL LAND TRACT SALES — A PURCHASE, AND NEVER A RESIDENCE. The Illinois State Archives' Public Domain Land Tract Sales register enters this person 3 times, as “KINZIE ROBERT A”, “KINZIE ROBERT”, 1830-09-27 to 1831-05-07: 1 federal land entry — NFRSC sec 10 T39N R14E and 2 lots in the platted town — lot 3 of block 35 in the town the register codes CHIOT (L3BL35CHIOT, as printed); lot 5 of block 35 in the town the register codes CHIOT (L5BL35CHIOT, as printed), 102.29 acres stated in all, for $185.86 (ls0059, ls1315, ls1316). THE REGISTER'S OWN RESIDENCE COLUMN READS COOK, UNKNOWN on these rows: a county, a state or nothing, and never a town, which is why a purchase here places nobody. THE TOWN LOTS ARE THE PLAT ITSELF, AND THEY ARE NOT ACRES: Cook County's register describes them by lot and block in a platted town and gives them no section, no township and no acreage at all, so they add nothing to the acre figure above and $58.00 to the money. This project does not expand the register's town codes, so which addition a lot stands in is carried as the code and not as a name. It is still a purchase and it still places nobody. The register states this purchaser's residence as COOK, so the sale is contemporary evidence that a man of this name lived in Cook County on the date of sale. It is not evidence that he lived in the town. A purchase and nothing more. It dates and places a transaction; it proposes no residence, and under the ratified ladder it corroborates rather than mints. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: KINZIE ROBERT A matches Robert Allen Kinzie: the forename names Robert Allen Kinzie of the 4 people of this surname, and the forename agrees in full. (data/research/land_sales/resident_crosswalk.json). This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE. Under the ratified ladder (T-0513) a second independent source is what lifts a projected resident, and a land entry is a second source about a TRANSACTION rather than about who was living at Chicago on 1 July 1835 — a man may buy a quarter-section he never sees. T-0515 applies the ladder against every source at once; this pass hands it the evidence and not the verdict.

research_note: A MERCHANT WHOSE BUYING TRIP TO NEW YORK PUT THE TOWN ON THE MAP. This household is worth its place less for the man than for the mechanism it documents: in the winter of 1832-33 a Chicago trader buying Indian goods in a New York store is how eastern capital first heard that Chicago was worth buying. The population curve K1 is reconstructing starts there.

directories.note: LATER EVIDENCE, BESIDE THE 1835 CLAIMS AND NOT INSIDE THEM. A Chicago directory of 1839, 1843 or 1844 meets somebody of this name and this pass records what it prints. Under the ratified ladder a directory read after 1835 can corroborate that a person attested here was still in Chicago and can print a trade or a street the 1835 record never had; on its own it makes nobody a resident of 1835. Nothing on this person's 1835 record was regraded, moved, dated or given an occupation by this entry. WHAT THIS PASS RULED ONTO THIS HOUSEHOLD, named so the ruling can be found again: each volume below is followed by the printed entries it set against this person and the status the crosswalk ruled them at — a single entry carries what its own `could_carry` declares, and an ambiguous or contested match carries nothing and is shown so that the silence is legible. kinzie_robert_a, Fergus's Chicago directory of 1839 — f1839_e0863 (a single entry); kinzie_robert_a, Fergus's Chicago directory of 1843 — f1843_e1502 (a single entry).

address_later.note: Fergus's Chicago directory of 1839 prints this address against this person, in the entry quoted on the card: 'Kinzie, Robert A., Davis, Kinzie & Hyde, Kinzie street'. It is evidence about 1839, written here as 1839's and read back onto no 1835 claim. Under the ratified ladder a directory read after 1835 can corroborate that a person attested here was still in Chicago and can print a trade or a street the 1835 record never had; on its own it makes nobody a resident of 1835. Nothing on this person's 1835 record was regraded, moved, dated or given an occupation by this entry. The value is the volume's own line, split by its crosswalk on the entry's punctuation. These volumes set the trade first and its qualifiers after it on the same line, so the split may carry an employer, a market or a corner along with the trade. The printed entry is quoted beside the value for exactly that reason: the split is checkable against it, and neither is read into an 1835 claim.

back_projection.note: NOT READ BACK, BECAUSE SOMETHING BETTER ALREADY STANDS. Fergus's Chicago directory of 1839 prints an address against this name in 1839, and it is left where it is. An 1835 placement already stands: this household works at `robert_kinzie_store`, and clause 2 says an attested 1835 placement always beats a door printed 4 years later. The later address stays on the record as 1839's evidence and moves nothing.
